Sugriva Crowned; the Monsoon Wait

Stories from the Ramayana

Sugriva Crowned; the Monsoon Wait

A King's Crown, and Four Months of Waiting on Mount Prasravana

In everyday English — Kishkindha Kanda, sargas 26–30

Stories by Eku

How to Read · · BEFORE WE BEGIN

Read aloud. This story is made to be told. Read slowly, as if you are sitting with everyone at home and telling it to them.

The yellow boxes are the characters speaking in their own words. Change your voice a little as you speak — Rama calm, Lakshmana affectionate, Hanuman sweet and wise, Sugriva joyful.

(The purple cues) tell you where to pause, whisper, or raise your voice. They are for the reader — do not read them aloud.

At the end of every part is a green box — Pause and think. Stop there. Ask the question. Let the listeners speak.

The heart of this book is the description of the rains and the autumn. Read the fourth and sixth parts slowly, as if you yourself are watching the rain, then watching a clear autumn morning. Valmiki wrote the seasons as if they were alive.

The main story of this book is from the Valmiki Ramayana, Kishkindha Kanda, sargas 26–30. Anything more you may want to know is given separately at the end, in Where This Story Comes From.

Who's Who · · WHO'S WHO

Rama — the young prince of Ayodhya. Tall, calm, kind. Warm dark-brown skin, black hair tied back, simple gold jewellery, a bow in his hand. In the forest he walks barefoot, his upper cloth worn.

Lakshmana — Rama's younger brother. Like Rama, but a little shorter and lighter in colour. Bow in hand, simple green-beige forest dress, barefoot.

Sugriva — the new king of the vanaras, son of the Sun. Warm brown fur, royal bearing. Having defeated Vali, he has won back his kingdom.

Angada — son of Vali, nephew of Sugriva. Young, brave, as strong as his father. Now he has been made crown prince.

Hanuman — the powerful vanara, light golden-brown fur, long tail, gentle devoted face, saffron dhoti. Sugriva's wisest minister.

Jambavan — the old bear-king, the eldest and wisest companion of the vanaras.

Tara — wife of Vali, now with Sugriva. Wise and calm.

Gaja, Gavaksha, Gavaya, Sharabha, Gandhamadana, Mainda, Dvivida, Nila — vanara heroes and commanders, who pour the water at the coronation.

1 · Preparing the Coronation · · PREPARING THE CORONATION

Vali had been killed — and Sugriva had won back his kingdom. Now came the time — for the coronation.

Hanuman said, “Rama, Sugriva's coronation should happen before you. You yourself should make him king.”

But Rama said, “Hanuman, I am in exile. During exile I cannot enter a village or a city. Therefore you, the vanara chiefs, shall perform the coronation.”

Rama said: “And one more thing — make Angada the crown prince too. He is the eldest son of your elder brother, his valour is like his father's. He is the right choice for the crown-prince-ship.”

Rama went on — “Sugriva, listen — the four months of the rainy season have begun. This is Shravana — the first month of the rains, which brings many showers. This is not a time for striving.”

“Therefore enter the blessed city of Kishkindha — and I shall stay on this mountain with Lakshmana. The cave of this mountain is spacious and breezy, there is much water here, and red and blue lotuses aplenty.”

Rama said: “When the month of Kartika comes — after the rains — you shall do your best in the cause of Ravana's destruction. That is our covenant. For now, go to your palace, sit in your kingdom, and gladden your friends.”

Sugriva obeyed Rama's words. Now the preparations for the coronation began — in Kishkindha, by Rama's command, at the hands of the vanara chiefs.

Pause and think — Rama refused to have the coronation done before him — because in exile he could not enter a city. Does this show that Rama held his word — the rules of exile — above even the joy of crowning a king? And he spoke of making Angada the crown prince — does this show that he wanted to give even his enemy's son his rightful due?

2 · Sugriva's Coronation · · SUGRIVA'S CORONATION

In Kishkindha the coronation was prepared — as the coronation of a great king is prepared.

First the Brahmans learned in the Vedas were pleased with jewels, garments and delicious food. Then ritual grass was spread around the fire-altar — and the sacred fire was kindled, and oblations offered into it with hymns.

Then Sugriva was seated on a splendid, choicest throne — with legs of gold, set upon a high platform decorated with garlands of flowers. He sat facing east — and the chanting of Vedic hymns began.

Then the vanara heroes — Gaja, Gavaksha, Gavaya, Sharabha, Gandhamadana, Mainda, Dvivida, Hanuman and Jambavan — began to pour pure water upon Sugriva.

Where had that water come from? From the rivers flowing to the east and to the west, from the sacred banks of rivers, and from every ocean — and it had been stored in golden flasks.

As they poured the water, the vanara heroes looked as if the gods themselves were anointing a king.

Then Sugriva embraced Angada — and, as Rama had said, made him crown prince.

Kishkindha — already splendid with flags of triumph and banners — shone still further. Joyful and strong monkeys spread through the whole city.

Sugriva was now king of the vanara army. He sent the news to Rama — and Rama, hearing it, was pleased.

Pause and think — The water for the coronation came from everywhere — rivers of the east and west, sacred banks, every ocean. Does this show that a king's kingdom is not of one city alone — but of all directions? And Sugriva embraced Angada — does this show that even after winning a kingdom, embracing one's family comes first?

3 · Mount Prasravana · · MOUNT PRASRAVANA

Sugriva's coronation was done — and he entered the cave-city of Kishkindha.

Rama and Lakshmana — the two brothers — reached Mount Prasravana. That mountain is also called Malyavat.

What was that mountain like? Tigers and wild beasts growled in it, lions roared, shrubs and creepers were thick, there were many kinds of trees — and bears, monkeys, baboons and wildcats lived there. That mountain was always holy and tranquil — and in its shine it was like a heap of clouds.

Rama and Lakshmana made a spacious cave on the cliff of that mountain their home.

Rama said: “Lakshmana, this cave is spacious and breezy — we shall stay here during the rainy nights.”

Rama went on — “Look, the peak of this mountain is embellished with white, black and coppery rock faces — and there are many kinds of ores here. And Sugriva's beautiful Kishkindha is not very far from here.”

Rama thought — “Sugriva has won back his wife, he has won his kingdom — surrounded by his friends, he must surely be joyful.”

But in Rama's heart there was no joy. He was separated from Sita — and that separation was eating at his heart.

Lakshmana saw this — and comforted Rama.

Lakshmana said: “Brother, look forward to the autumn. Sugriva will do all that you desire — and soon. Bear this time of rain — and spend these four rainy months on this mountain as a monsoon lion spends them.”

Rama accepted Lakshmana's words — “I shall wait for the autumn — when the rivers grow calm, and Sugriva is pleased.”

Pause and think — Rama thought of Sugriva's joy — but he himself had no joy. Does this show that when we are separated from one of our own, even the joy of others gives us no joy? And what did Lakshmana do — he did not preach to Rama, but said: wait, Sugriva will do it. Is this the way to comfort — to give hope, not a sermon?

4 · The Monsoon Described · · THE MONSOON DESCRIBED

Having killed Vali and crowned Sugriva — Rama was living on Mount Prasravana. And one day he said to Lakshmana, “Lakshmana, look — the rains have come.”

The sky — the sky was fully covered with clouds like mountains. (Read this slowly — as if you yourself are looking at the sky.)

Rama said, “Having drunk the essence of the oceans through the Sun's rays, the sky sustained a nine-month pregnancy — and now it is giving birth to the elixir of life.”

“One may climb the stairs of clouds and garland the sun with garlands of kutaja and arjuna flowers — such are these days.”

The clouds looked as if soft bandages had been tied on the gashes of the sky — white at the edges, tinged with the red of sunset. The sluggish breeze was like their sighs, the sunset like sandal paste upon them — and the sky seemed like one sighing in love.

And the earth — the earth scorched by summer, wetted by new waters — looked like Sita, searing with grief and outpouring tears.

The breezes freed from the wombs of clouds — cool as the leaves of camphor, perfumed with ketaki — were such that one could drink them from the bowl of one's palms.

And the mountain — in full bloom with arjuna flowers, fragranced with ketaki — was being anointed with downpours, as Sugriva was anointed when his enemy was silenced.

The mountains looked like young scholars reciting the Vedas — the clouds their black deerskins, the showers their sacred threads, and the caves full of breeze their voices.

Lightning was whipping the sky as if with golden whips — and the sky was letting out the rattle of thunder, bearing its inner throes.

And that lightning — squirming on the blue cloud — seemed to Rama like woeful Vaidehi squirming in the grasp of Ravana.

Rama said, “Lakshmana, look — the directions have grown unclear. For those who have their beloveds with them, this is good — but for one loverless like me, it is hard.”

Kutaja flowers bloomed on the terraces of the mountain — covered with drops of vapour, like tears of happiness on the face of a beloved when her lover arrives.

The dust had quietened, the breeze had grown chilly, the evils of summer had quietened. The conquests of kings had come to a halt — and people living abroad were returning to their own countries.

The swans had started for Lake Manasa — but the chakravaka birds stayed with their beloveds. Carts were not moving on the roads battered by rain.

The sky was bright somewhere, dark somewhere else — like a vast tideless ocean dammed up by cloud-mountains.

The mountain streams — mingled with sarja and kadamba flowers, coppery with the ores of the mountain — were flowing swiftly, and peacocks screamed behind them.

The jambu fruits — like bees, full of juice — were being eaten with delight. And the over-ripe mangoes — shaken by the wind — were falling to the ground.

The clouds — with lightning as their flags, with cranes as their garlands, like the pinnacles of lordly mountains — were thundering like maddened lordly elephants standing up to a fight.

The pasturelands satiated with rainwater — and the dancing carnivals of peacocks in the afternoons — made the woodlands more splendid still.

The clouds — heavy with water, adorned with cranes, rumbling — were resting and resting again on the loftiest mountain peaks as they travelled, like pregnant women.

Rows of cranes — flying all over, desirous of the clouds, highly delighted — shone like lovely festoons of white lotus flowers dangled upon the sky by the wind.

The meadowland with its new meadows — dappled within with young red indragopa beetles — shone like a woman wearing a parrot-green wraparound embroidered with lac-red spots.

These days sleep was slowly approaching Vishnu, rivers were rapidly approaching the ocean, cranes were gleefully approaching the clouds — and women were passionately approaching their beloveds.

The interiors of the forests were fit for peacocks to dance, the kadamba trees were in bloom with their branches, bulls were with cows — and the earth, with its crops and orchards, had become delightful.

Rivers were surging, clouds were showering, rutty elephants were trumpeting, the forest interiors were shining, the loverless were reminiscing, peacocks were dancing — and the monkeys were resolving to stay in one place.

On whiffing the fragrance of ketaki flowers, the lordly elephants were highly joyous — but they were baffled by the sounds of waterfalls in the forest streams — and they blared together with the screaming peacocks.

Honeybees languishing on the branches of kadamba trees — knocked down by the downpour of rain — were slowly losing the intoxication they had gained in a moment by plunging into the nectar of flowers.

The branches of jambu trees — laden with fruits like heaps of coal powder, full of abundant juice — shone as if swilled by hives of honeybees.

A lordly elephant — walking towards the forest along the mountain track — heard the thundering of a cloud, and mistook it for the war-cry of another elephant. He turned right about — eager for a head-on collision!

Somewhere the interiors of the forests were singing with swarms of honeybees, elsewhere they were dancing with purple-necked peacocks, somewhere else they were excited with lordly elephants — and the forests shone as a retreat for many bees, birds and animals.

Pause and think — Rama described the rains — the sky, the earth, the mountain, the clouds, the peacocks, the elephants, the honeybees. Is rain only water — or does it change everything — the earth, the air, the animals, and the heart too? And Rama saw Sita in everything — in the earth, in the lightning. When one of our own is far away, does everything show us that person?

5 · Hanuman Reminds Sugriva · · HANUMAN REMINDS SUGRIVA

Meanwhile in Kishkindha — Sugriva, having won kingdom and glory — had sunk into lavish enjoyment.

He had regained his wife, he had gained Tara — and he lived day and night in delight, as Indra lives with gandharvas and apsaras. He had left the work of the kingdom to his ministers — and he did not even look at those ministers.

Time passed — and Sugriva forgot his promise. That promise — which he had given Rama — the promise of the search for Sita.

Then Hanuman saw — the sky had cleared, the lightning and clouds had gone, the sarasa birds were bustling, and delightful moonshine was spread over everything.

Hanuman went to Sugriva — and spoke in sweet, reasonable, heart-pleasing words.

Hanuman said: “Great king, the kingdom is won, glory is won, the prosperity of your house has grown — but gathering your friends still remains. He who conducts himself punctually and amiably with friends — his kingdom, glory and valour flourish.”

Hanuman said: “He whose treasury, army, friends and self — all four — are in balance, enjoys a matchless kingdom. Therefore do your friend's work dutifully — the work for which Rama and Lakshmana came to you.”

Hanuman said: “He who belatedly serves his friend's mission is not joined to that mission, even if he has done great deeds. The task of our friend — the search for Vaidehi — is delayed. Rama, knower of time, though hurrying, says nothing to you — because he abides by your promise.”

Sugriva heard Hanuman's words — and he awoke. He ordered Nila, “Gather all the monkey troops within fifteen days.”

Then he went back into his inner palace chambers — but now Rama's work was in his heart.

Pause and think — Sugriva had sunk into pleasure — and forgotten his promise. Can pleasure sometimes make us forget a promise? And what did Hanuman do — he did not scold Sugriva, but explained in sweet and reasonable words. Is this the right way to wake someone — not to scold, but to explain? And Hanuman said — to be late in a friend's work is also wrong. Is helping on time also dharma?

6 · Autumn Arrives · · AUTUMN ARRIVES

The rains had passed — and autumn had arrived.

Thousand-eyed Indra, having propitiated the earth with waters and conferred abundant crops, stood accomplished. The clouds had poured all their water — and now they had calmed.

The clouds — having assumed a lighter shade of black, spread thinly over the trees and mountains — were quiet, like elephants who have lost their pride. The wind carried the fragrance of kutaja and arjuna flowers.

The trumpets of the elephants and the screams of the peacocks had gone quiet. The mountain peaks — cleaned by the downpour — shone in the colour of their minerals.

The saptachhada trees were full of bloom — and the bees buzzed around them. The radiance of the sun, the moon and the stars flooded the earth. The gentle breeze made the elephants sport.

The rays of the sun had made the lotuses bloom — as if inviting Lakshmi. Lotuses had bloomed on the rivers — and the chakravaka birds and swans revelled on them, spreading the pollen.

The branches of the forest were loaded with golden blooms — and bent with their weight.

Rama was sitting on the mountain — he saw the clear autumn sky, in which sarasa cranes were flying and cackling. At once his mind went to Sita.

Rama said: “Sita used to revel in the cackle of the sarasa cranes in the hermitage. She used to wake to the cackle of the swans. The chakravaka birds were her companions — she was delighted to hear their cackles. Alas! Even my delicate darling must be getting scorched by the pleasant autumn, bereft of me.”

Rama cried pitiably, like a chakravaka bird crying and pleading to Lord Indra for rain.

Then Lakshmana — who had gone to fetch forest produce and fruits — returned. He saw his elder brother in grief — and consoled him.

The rains had passed. Autumn had come. And now — the time for the search for Sita had come.

Pause and think — Autumn had come — the sky clear, the lotuses blooming, the sarasa birds flying. But in Rama's heart there was no joy — because Sita was not with him. Does the beauty of a season also seem pale when one of our own is not with us? And Lakshmana came again — with fruits, with consolation. Is a brother's company the greatest consolation of all?

Bigger Thoughts · · BIGGER THOUGHTS

In this tale there are two seasons — the rains and the autumn. And two hearts — Rama's, waiting; and Sugriva's, sunk in pleasure and forgetting his promise.

Rama described the rains — the sky, the earth, the mountain, the clouds, the peacocks, the elephants — and in everything he saw Sita. Sugriva found pleasure — but in pleasure he forgot his promise. And Hanuman woke him — with sweet words.

Ask the listeners:

1. Rama described the rains — and saw Sita in everything. When one of our own is far away, does everything show us that person?

2. In the rains the conquests of kings halted, and travellers returned home. Does rain stop everything — or does it bring everyone home?

3. Sugriva sank into pleasure — and forgot his promise. Can pleasure sometimes make us forget a promise?

4. Hanuman did not scold Sugriva — he explained in sweet and reasonable words. Is this the right way to wake someone?

5. Hanuman said — to be late in a friend's work is also wrong. Is helping on time also dharma?

6. Autumn had come — the sky clear, the lotuses blooming, the sarasa birds flying. But in Rama's heart there was no joy. Does the beauty of a season also seem pale when one of our own is not with us?

7. Lakshmana consoled Rama twice — once in the rains, once in the autumn. Is a brother's company the greatest consolation of all?

Where This Story Comes From · · WHERE THIS STORY COMES FROM

Main Source

The main story of this book is from the Valmiki Ramayana, Kishkindha Kanda, sargas 26–30 — Sugriva's coronation, the rainy season on Mount Prasravana, Hanuman's reminder, and the arrival of autumn.

Preparing the Coronation — Sarga 26

Hanuman's proposal of the coronation before Rama, Rama's inability to enter a city during exile, his asking the vanara chiefs to perform it, his suggestion to make Angada crown prince, Shravana — the first month of the rains — and the promise of the destruction of Ravana in Kartika — this is in sarga 26.

Sugriva's Coronation — Sarga 26

Pleasing the Brahmans with jewels, garments and food, spreading ritual grass around the fire-altar and offering oblations with hymns, seating Sugriva facing east on a throne with golden legs, Gaja, Gavaksha, Gavaya, Sharabha, Gandhamadana, Mainda, Dvivida, Hanuman and Jambavan pouring water brought from the rivers of east and west, the sacred banks and the oceans in golden flasks, Sugriva embracing Angada and making him crown prince, and Kishkindha splendid with flags and banners — this is in sarga 26.

Mount Prasravana — Sarga 27

Rama and Lakshmana reaching Mount Prasravana (Malyavat) — tigers, lions, shrubs, creepers, many kinds of trees, bears, monkeys, baboons, wildcats, a shine like a heap of clouds — the spacious breezy cave on the cliff, the white, black and coppery rock faces, Kishkindha nearby, Rama thinking of Sugriva's joy and finding no joy himself, Lakshmana's consolation — waiting for autumn, spending the four rainy months like a monsoon lion — this is in sarga 27.

The Monsoon Described — Sarga 28

Rama's long description of the rains — the sky covered with mountain-like clouds, heaven sustaining a nine-month pregnancy through the Sun's rays and giving birth to the elixir of life, climbing the stairs of clouds to garland the sun with kutaja and arjuna flowers, clouds like bandages on the gashes of the sky, the sky sighing like a lover, the earth like Sita outpouring tears, breezes cool as camphor and perfumed with ketaki, the mountain anointed like Sugriva, mountains like young scholars reciting the Vedas, lightning like golden whips, lightning like Sita in Ravana's grasp, the unclear directions, the kutaja flowers, the quietened dust, the halted conquests, the swans going to Lake Manasa, the carts halted on battered roads, the sky like a tideless ocean, the coppery streams with sarja and kadamba flowers, the jambu and mango fruits, the clouds like war-elephants, the peacocks dancing in the afternoons, the clouds like pregnant women, the cranes like festoons of white lotuses, the meadow like a woman in a parrot-green wraparound, sleep approaching Vishnu, the peacocks' dance, the elephants joyous at ketaki, the bees knocked from kadamba branches, the jambu branches, the elephant turning at the thunder, the forest singing with bees, peacocks and elephants — this is in sarga 28.

Hanuman's Reminder — Sarga 29

Sugriva sinking into pleasure after winning kingdom and glory, regaining his wife and gaining Tara, merrymaking day and night, leaving the kingdom to his ministers, Hanuman seeing the clear sky and the bustling sarasa birds and approaching Sugriva, explaining in sweet and reasonable words — gathering friends remains, he who is punctual with friends prospers, the balance of treasury, army, friends and self, belated service to a friend's mission, the delayed search for Vaidehi, Rama hurrying yet saying nothing — and Sugriva ordering Nila to gather the monkey troops within fifteen days — this is in sarga 29.

Autumn Arrives — Sarga 30

The passing of the rains, Indra propitiating the earth with waters and conferring crops, the clouds calming, the wind with the fragrance of kutaja and arjuna, the quieting of elephants and peacocks, the peaks shining in the colour of their minerals, the saptachhada trees in bloom and the bees, the radiance of sun, moon and stars, the lotuses blooming and inviting Lakshmi, the chakravaka birds and swans spreading pollen, the branches bent with golden blooms, Rama seeing the sarasa cranes in the clear autumn sky and remembering Sita — her delight in the cranes' cackle in the hermitage, waking to the swans, the chakravaka companions — and Lakshmana returning with fruits and consoling him — this is in sarga 30.

Prasravana and Malyavat

Mount Prasravana is also called Malyavat — the mountain where Rama and Lakshmana spent the rainy season.

What Happens Next

The vanara army will gather — and parties will go in the four directions to search for Sita. Rama will give Hanuman his signet ring. That tale is in the next books of this series.

The End · · THE END

Here the tale of Sugriva's coronation and the rainy season comes to rest — a king's crown, four months of waiting on a mountain, the description of the rains, Hanuman's reminder, and the arrival of autumn.

And whenever the rains come — remember Rama's description — the clouds, the peacocks, the elephants, and the earth shedding tears like Sita. And whenever autumn comes — remember that clear sky, in which the sarasa birds flew — and Rama remembered Sita.

— The End —
